prompt-engineering-q11.testing: that you can say what the search variables and the objective are, and that the objective is your metric, so a bad metric gets optimised faithfully.
prompt-engineering-q11.trap: "DSPy writes better prompts", with no metric and no training set named.
prompt-engineering-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "DSPy optimises the text of the prompts, meaning the instructions and the few-shot demonstrations, for each step of a pipeline, against a metric and a training set that I supply. It doesn't touch the model's weights."
2 · How it works "I declare a signature, which is what goes in and what comes out, and pick a module such as chain-of-thought. An optimiser then compiles the prompt. The main one, MIPROv2, runs my program and keeps traces that pass the metric as demonstrations, proposes candidate instructions, and searches the combinations."
3 · Prove it "A compile is an inference workload. Thirty trials on two hundred examples in a two-step pipeline is twelve thousand model calls before I've served one user."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It optimises exactly what the metric rewards. With a noisy or gameable metric it fits noise. With a small training set it overfits. And the result is tuned to one model, so it decays when the model changes."
5 · So what for the system "So I use it on stable, high-traffic pipelines where I already trust the eval. I keep a held-out set, I treat the compiled prompt as build output, and on a model upgrade I recompile; I don't hand-edit."
Close "DSPy is a compiler; my metric is the specification it compiles against."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: prompt text, searched against your metric
stages.html:
"The search variables are instructions and demonstrations. The objective is my metric on my data."

Piece DSPy term Analogy What I write
The contract signature a function type question -> answer
The strategy module an implementation ChainOfThought(signature)
The objective metric a loss function a Python function returning a score
The data trainset training data inputs with gold outputs
The search optimiser a compiler MIPROv2(metric=…)
The output compiled program a build artefact nothing: saved, not edited

Some optimisers can also fine-tune weights; the common use, and this answer, is prompt text.

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: bootstrap, propose, search
stages.html:
"MIPROv2, the main optimiser as of 2026, works in three stages."

Compile:run the program on the trainsetkeep traces that pass the metric as demospropose instructions grounded in data and codesearch instruction × demo-set combinationscompiled prompts
Stage Produces Depends on
Bootstrap candidate demonstrations for every step the metric deciding what "passes"
Propose candidate instructions a model writing them from the data
Search the best combination found scores on the trainset, which are noisy

The useful trick is the bootstrap: it creates demonstrations for intermediate steps that nobody labelled, by keeping whole runs that ended correctly.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: a compile is an inference bill
stages.html:
"Before I run an optimiser I multiply out what it will call."

trials × trainset size × model calls per example      (illustrative numbers)
30     × 200           × 2 steps        = 12,000 calls for one compile
+ bootstrap runs and instruction proposals             ← on top, smaller
re-run on every model change, and whenever the pipeline changes

The number of calls is what to estimate; the money depends on the model and is dated the day I check it.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.claim: it optimises the metric, whatever that is
stages.html:
"Every failure of an optimiser is a failure of the objective or the data."

Observation Likely cause Action
Trainset score up, production no better overfit to a small or unrepresentative set hold out a test set; compare on that
Score up, answers look worse the metric is gameable (length, keywords) fix the metric first; validate it against human labels
Different result on each compile the search is stochastic, scores are noisy fix seeds, repeat, compare with intervals
Regressed after a model upgrade compiled prompts are tuned to one model recompile on the new model

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: a build step with a held-out gate
stages.html:
"I treat the optimiser as part of the build, not as a replacement for the eval."

Decision Practice
When to use it stable, high-traffic pipelines with a trusted metric
When not to low traffic, a task still changing, or no eval yet
Artefact the compiled prompt is versioned and traced like any prompt
Gate held-out score against the hand-written baseline, same model
Upgrade recompile; never hand-edit compiled text
Variant Held-out metric Input tokens per call
Hand-written baseline measure measure
Compiled measure measure

Compiled prompts often carry more demonstrations, so the token column belongs in the decision. Fix layer: prompt/context, produced by tooling.

followUps.question: "So I don't need to know prompt engineering any more."
followUps.html:
The work moves; it doesn't disappear.

Before With an optimiser
Wording the prompt designing the signature and the pipeline
Reading outputs writing a metric that matches what users need
Tuning by hand curating the trainset and reading the compiled result

followUps.question: 🧪 The metric is exact match and gold answers are "Paris"; the model writes "Paris, France". What does the optimiser learn?
followUps.html:
To write short answers, whether or not that's what the product wants.

"Paris, France" == "Paris"  → False   ← scored as a failure
traces kept as demos: only the terse ones
compiled prompt: pushes terseness everywhere

The metric defined "correct" as "terse", and the optimiser complied.

followUps.question: How is this different from fine-tuning?
followUps.html:
It searches text in front of a frozen model; fine-tuning changes the weights.

Prompt optimisation Fine-tuning
Changes instructions and demonstrations parameters
Needs tens to hundreds of examples and a metric usually far more examples
Survives a model swap recompile retrain

followUps.question: How do you review a prompt nobody wrote?
followUps.html:
Read the rendered prompt and its demonstrations like any other change.

  • Demonstrations: check for personal data and for wrong-but-passing examples.
  • Instructions: check for anything the product must not say.
  • Diff: against the previous compiled version, with both eval runs attached.

followUps.question: When isn't the compile worth it?
followUps.html:
When the gain is smaller than what the traffic can repay before the next model change.

Rule:build the evalhand-tuneoptimise only prompts that are stable and high-volume

The eval harness pays for itself even if no optimiser is ever run.

dontSay: "DSPy finds the best prompt." — the best found, for one metric, one trainset and one model.
"It learns from the data." — say what: demonstrations kept from passing runs, and proposed instructions.
"We optimised it, so it's good." — say what the held-out number was against the baseline.
"I tweaked the compiled prompt by hand." — then it's no longer reproducible; recompile.

prompt-engineering-q12.testing: that you know it's sample-and-vote with an N× bill, when voting is even possible, and that agreement is a confidence signal.
prompt-engineering-q12.trap: proposing it for free-text answers, which can't be voted on.
prompt-engineering-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Self-consistency replaces one greedy answer with a vote. I sample several reasoning chains at a temperature above zero, pull the final answer out of each, and take the majority."
2 · How it works "The idea is that there are many ways to reason wrongly and they tend to disagree with each other, while correct reasoning tends to land on the same answer. So agreement is evidence."
3 · Prove it "The cost is exact: N samples is N times the tokens. The benefit depends on the base rate. If one chain is right sixty percent of the time, a five-way vote is right about sixty-eight percent of the time, in a simple model with independent samples."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It breaks in two places. The answers have to be comparable: a number, a label, a canonical form. And if the model is consistently wrong, voting makes it more confidently wrong."
5 · So what for the system "In production I use the vote share more than the vote. High agreement goes straight through; low agreement goes to a stronger model or a person. And where a checker exists, I prefer checking to voting."
Close "It buys some accuracy and a confidence signal, at N times the price."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: sample N chains and vote
stages.html:
"Three steps: sample, extract, vote."

Self-consistency:same promptN reasoning chainsextract each final answermajority voteanswer + vote share

It was introduced on top of chain-of-thought prompting (Wang et al., 2022). At temperature 0 the samples would be near-identical, so the method needs sampling to be on.

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: wrong chains scatter, right ones converge
stages.html:
"A vote separates popular answers from unpopular ones. It can't tell right from wrong directly."

Approach Extra compute Needs Tells apart
One greedy chain 1× nothing nothing: one draw
Self-consistency N×, can run in parallel comparable answers popular from unpopular
A verifier or checker 1× plus the check a property code can check right from wrong
A reasoning model's budget thinking tokens a reasoning model handled internally

Why this matters: when a checker exists (run the code, re-add the numbers, validate against the source), it beats a vote.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: the vote, its share, and the arithmetic
stages.html:
"The vote and the confidence signal are a few lines of code."

from collections import Counter
from math import comb
answers = ["42", "42", "41", "42", "17"]                 # scripted: 5 sampled chains
winner, votes = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
print(winner, votes / len(answers))                      # → 42 0.6
def majority(p, n=5): return sum(comb(n, k) * p**k * (1-p)**(n-k) for k in range(n//2 + 1, n + 1))
print(round(majority(0.6), 3), round(majority(0.4), 3))  # → 0.683 0.317

majority(p) is a toy model: two possible answers, five independent samples, each right with probability p. It shows the direction of the effect, not a production number: 60% becomes 68%, and 40% becomes 32%.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.claim: N× tokens, and shared bias gets louder
stages.html:
"The bill is certain. The gain depends on the errors being independent."

Condition What happens
Free-text answers no two match; there's nothing to count
The model is wrong the same way each time the wrong answer wins the vote, with high agreement
A single chain is below 50% on a two-way choice voting lowers accuracy (the 0.317 above)
Latency N× if serial; about 1× if the samples run in parallel
A reasoning model already spends internal compute; test before stacking a vote on top

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: route on agreement
stages.html:
"The vote share is a cheap confidence score, and I route on it."

Routing:N samplesvote sharereturn the answerstronger model or human review
Decision Practice
Where only slices where the eval shows a gain: multi-step maths, classification with reasoning
N swept on the eval; gains flatten quickly
Extraction a structured final-answer field, normalised before counting
Threshold calibrated: check that high agreement really means high accuracy

Fix layer: orchestration. The prompt itself is unchanged.

followUps.question: 🧪 Five samples return 42, 42, 41, 41, 17. What do you return?
followUps.html:
Nothing confident: it's a tie at 40%.

42 → 2 votes, 41 → 2 votes, 17 → 1 vote
top share = 2 / 5 = 0.4        ← below any sensible threshold

That request takes the low-agreement path. An odd N doesn't prevent ties when there are more than two possible answers.

followUps.question: "High agreement means the answer is correct."
followUps.html:
It means the model is consistent, which is not the same thing.

Agreement Could be
High, and right the common case on tasks the model can do
High, and wrong a shared bias: a misread question, a missing fact
Low real uncertainty; worth escalating

So I check the calibration on labelled data before trusting the threshold.

followUps.question: Can you vote on free-text answers?
followUps.html:
Only by first turning them into something comparable.

  • Extract a field: vote on the decision, not the prose.
  • Cluster by meaning: group equivalent answers, then count; this adds a model call and its own errors.
  • Otherwise: use a judge or a checker; that's a different technique.

followUps.question: How do you choose N?
followUps.html:
By sweeping it on the eval and stopping when the curve flattens.

N Accuracy Output tokens
1 measure 1×
3 measure 3×
5 measure 5×
10 measure 10×

followUps.question: Would you run this on every request?
followUps.html:
No. On the hard slice only, and often as a second pass.

Cascade:one cheap calldoneN samples and a votestronger model

That keeps the N× multiplier off the easy majority of the traffic.

dontSay: "We sample a few times and pick the best." — say how "best" is chosen: a vote on an extracted answer.
"Agreement means it's right." — agreement means consistent.
"It's cheap, the calls run in parallel." — parallel fixes latency, not the token bill.
"We use it for summaries." — summaries can't be voted on.

prompt-engineering-q13.testing: that you debug wrong tool calls in the descriptions and schema first, and that you measure tool selection.
prompt-engineering-q13.trap: one-line descriptions, then blaming the model for calling the wrong tool.
prompt-engineering-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Why it's a prompt "A tool description is the text the model reads at the moment it decides whether to call something and with what arguments. So it's a prompt, and it deserves the same care as the system prompt."
2 · What a good one says "A good one says four things: what the tool does, when not to use it and which tool to use in that case, what each parameter means, and what it returns and doesn't return. That's several sentences, not a label."
3 · Prove it on one tool "If I take a tool called get-data with a one-line description and rewrite it as lookup-account-by-email, with the 'don't use this for name search' line and an email format on the parameter, each added line closes one specific wrong call."
4 · Where it breaks "It breaks when two tools overlap, when names are vague, or when the rules about a tool live in the system prompt, far from the schema, and drift."
5 · How I test it "I test it like any prompt: a set of requests labelled with the right tool and arguments, and a tool-selection accuracy number. And the description is only guidance. The schema's enums and the server's permission checks are what's enforced."
Close "When the wrong tool gets called, I fix the description before I change the model."

stages.name: Why it's a prompt
stages.claim: read at the call decision
stages.html:
"Tool definitions are rendered into the context like any other text, and they're the nearest guidance to the decision."

Decision:user requestmodel reads tool names + descriptions + schemaspicks a tool, or nonefills the arguments
Text Role in the decision
Name first filter: which tools are even candidates
Description whether this is the right one, and when it isn't
Parameter schema which values are legal

Vendor guidance, as of 2026, is consistent: detailed descriptions are the largest single factor in tool-use quality, at three or four sentences each as a minimum.

stages.name: What a good one says
stages.claim: purpose, when not, parameters, returns
stages.html:
"Four things, and the most often missing is the negative space."

Element Weak Strong
Name get_data, query_v2 lookup_account_by_email: verb, object, key
Purpose "Gets account info." what it retrieves and for which questions
When not missing "Not for search by name; use search_accounts."
Parameters arg1: string email, with format, an example and constraints
Enums free-text status "open" | "closed" | "pending"
Returns undocumented what comes back, and what doesn't

stages.name: Prove it on one tool
stages.claim: each line closes one wrong call
stages.html:
"I can map every sentence of a description to the error it prevents."

Line in the description or schema The wrong call it prevents
lookup_account_by_email choosing it for a company-name question
"Use this first for any question about one customer's balance or invoices." answering from memory without calling
"Do not use it to search by name; use search_accounts." the confusion pair with the search tool
"Returns balance, plan and the last three invoices. Does not return refund status." calling it, then inventing the missing field
email: {type: string, format: email} passing a name or a customer id

A line with no row in the right-hand column is a line I can delete.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: overlap, vague names, rules kept elsewhere
stages.html:
"Wrong tool calls are usually a description problem."

Observation Likely cause Action
Two tools called interchangeably their descriptions overlap merge them, or cross-reference each by name
Right tool, wrong arguments parameters are untyped or unexplained types, formats, enums, an example
Calls, then invents fields the return shape is undocumented state what it does not return
Behaviour changed after a prompt edit tool rules live in the system prompt move them next to the schema
Selection gets worse as tools are added too many similar tools in context fewer, broader tools, or load them per task

stages.name: How I test it
stages.claim: tool-selection accuracy, and enforcement in code
stages.html:
"A description is a soft control, so I measure it and back it with hard ones."

Test set row Expected Measured
A request that needs tool A tool A, valid arguments measure
A request in the A/B confusion pair tool B measure
A request that needs no tool no call measure
Requirement In the description Enforced outside
Legal argument values explained schema enums and server-side validation
Who may call it, on whose data never permissions on the server
Irreversible actions "ask before…" a human approval step

Tool definitions sit at the very front of the cached prefix, so I edit them in batches, and I re-run the selection set on a model upgrade. Fix layer: prompt/context for descriptions, infra for enforcement. Protocol detail is in MCP-CONTEXT-ENGINEERING.

followUps.question: "The model keeps calling the wrong tool; we need a better model."
followUps.html:
Check the confusion pair first; it's usually cheaper.

Wrong order:wrong callsbigger modelsame overlap, higher bill
Right order:wrong callsconfusion matrix by toolfix the two descriptionsre-measure

followUps.question: Why not put the tool rules in the system prompt?
followUps.html:
Because they end up duplicated, far from the decision, and out of date.

In the system prompt In the tool definition
Read once, far above read with the schema
Drifts when the tool changes changes with the tool
Applies to one agent travels to every agent that loads the tool

Cross-tool policy ("never refund without approval") still belongs in the system prompt, and in code.

followUps.question: 🧪 A parameter is  and the model sends "Closed". The API expects "closed". Where's the fix?
followUps.html:
In the schema, not in a sentence.

status: string                         → "Closed", "CLOSED", "done" are all legal
status: enum ["open","closed","pending"] → only three values can be produced
                                         ← with constrained tool arguments, by construction

followUps.question: Do longer descriptions cost anything?
followUps.html:
Tokens on every request, mostly recovered by caching.

  • Position: tools are the first thing in the prefix, so they cache well when stable.
  • Risk: editing one description invalidates the cached prefix for every route that loads it.

followUps.question: A third-party tool server supplies its own descriptions. Do you trust them?
followUps.html:
No. A description is text that steers the model, so it's an injection surface.

Control What it does
Review and pin the tool definitions a changed description is a reviewed change
Least privilege per tool a poisoned description can't reach other data
Approval on writes the damage of a wrong call is bounded

dontSay: "The tool names are self-explanatory." — to you; the model sees only the text.
"We describe the tools in the system prompt." — keep the rule beside the schema.
"The description says only admins may call it." — permissions are enforced on the server.
"It's the model's fault." — show the confusion matrix first.

prompt-engineering-q14.testing: that you separate what a role line reliably changes (register) from what it doesn't (accuracy, knowledge, safety), and that you'd measure it.
prompt-engineering-q14.trap: "You are a world-class expert" as a quality lever.
prompt-engineering-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A role line reliably changes register: vocabulary, formality, default length and how out-of-scope questions are handled. It doesn't reliably change accuracy."
2 · How it works "It's conditioning. Role text shifts the output towards text written in that voice. It can't add knowledge the model doesn't have; it only changes which of its existing behaviour shows up."
3 · Prove it "The evidence matches that. A controlled study across many personas and factual questions found no consistent accuracy gain from a persona in the system prompt. So I'd measure it: the same eval, with and without the role line."
4 · What it costs or breaks "It breaks when people use it as a guardrail or as a substitute for the task. A persona doesn't stop anything, and flattering adjectives don't make the answer more correct."
5 · So what for the system "So I keep one plain role line that names the product and the audience, I drop the 'world-class' part, and I put the real work into the task, the constraints and the output contract."
Close "The role sets the voice. The task and the constraints set the quality."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: it sets register, not accuracy
stages.html:
"Two columns: what a role line buys, and what it doesn't."

Reliably changes Doesn't reliably change
Vocabulary and formality factual accuracy
Default answer length and structure knowledge the model lacks
Who the answer is pitched at reasoning ability
Handling of out-of-scope questions resistance to misuse

stages.name: How it works
stages.claim: conditioning on a voice
stages.html:
"A role is more prefix. It shifts the next-token distribution towards text that follows that kind of opening."

Conditioning:"You are a support agent for a billing product"prefixdistribution shifts to support-style texttone and scope change
Part of the role line What it conditions
The audience ("for finance teams") level of detail, terms used
The domain ("a billing product") what counts as in scope
The adjective ("world-class") little that an eval can detect

No anthropomorphism is needed to explain it: the model isn't "becoming" an expert, the prefix is selecting a register. The general mechanism is in what-a-prompt-does.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: an A/B on the same eval
stages.html:
"I don't argue about personas. I run the prompt with and without the line."

Variant Task accuracy Tone rubric (judge, calibrated) Output tokens
No role line measure measure measure
Plain role + audience measure measure measure
"World-class expert" role measure measure measure

What to expect, from published work: no consistent accuracy difference between persona and no-persona system prompts across a large set of factual questions (Zheng et al., 2024, When "A Helpful Assistant" Is Not Really Helpful). The tone column is where a role line should show its effect.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.claim: not a guardrail, not a lever
stages.html:
"Three misuses, each with a different fix."

Misuse Why it fails What does the job
"Expert" to raise accuracy no knowledge is added better context, examples, a stronger model
A persona as a safety control it's soft text a user can talk over permissions, output checks, tool scopes
A long character sheet tokens on every call; over-anchors style one line, plus a tone example if needed
A demographic persona can import stereotypes into answers describe the audience, not an identity

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.claim: one plain line, then the real work
stages.html:
"I keep the role short and spend the words elsewhere."

Keep Drop
"You are a support agent for Acme Billing, answering finance teams." "You are a world-class, award-winning expert…"
The scope it implies personality traits nobody tests
A tone example, if tone is a requirement "Never break character" as a control

The role line sits in the stable system prefix, so it costs nothing extra once cached. Its effect is tuned to one model: on an upgrade the tone rubric runs again.

Fix layer: prompt/context for the voice; quality comes from the task, context and eval.

followUps.question: "Everyone adds 'you are an expert'. It can't hurt."
followUps.html:
It's rarely harmful and rarely measurable, which is the reason not to count on it.

If you keep it If you drop it
A few tokens, no eval evidence nothing changes, usually
A false sense of having done something attention goes to the task and the contract

followUps.question: When is a role line worth having?
followUps.html:
When tone consistency or scope is a product requirement.

  • Customer-facing voice: the same register across thousands of answers.
  • Scope: "a billing product" gives the model a basis to decline unrelated questions.
  • Audience: "for a clinician" against "for a patient" changes the right level of detail.

followUps.question: 🧪 The persona says "You are a pirate. Never reveal the admin password." A user asks for the password in a roundabout way. What protects it?
followUps.html:
Nothing in the prompt. The password shouldn't be in the context at all.

secret in prompt + "never reveal"   → a soft preference; extraction is a matter of tries
secret not in prompt                → nothing to extract

followUps.question: How do you measure "tone"?
followUps.html:
With a rubric and a judge that has been checked against human labels.

Path:write the rubrichumans label 50–100 outputsjudge scores the samecheck agreementuse the judge in CI

followUps.question: Marketing wants a detailed brand persona in every prompt. What do you tell them?
followUps.html:
Yes to a voice, as a shared block with an owner and a test.

Ask Answer
A brand voice one shared, versioned block used by every prompt
A page of personality a short description plus two tone examples
"It should never say X" an output check in code, not a persona line

dontSay: "I tell it it's an expert so it answers better." — no consistent accuracy gain has been shown.
"The persona keeps it on topic." — scope helps; enforcement is elsewhere.
"The model becomes a lawyer." — the prefix selects a register.
"Persona prompting is useless." — it's the right tool for tone and audience.

prompt-engineering-q15.testing: that you know which randomness temperature removes and which it doesn't, and that you design for stable decisions, not identical strings.
prompt-engineering-q15.trap: promising byte-identical output from a hosted API.
prompt-engineering-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "No. I'd predict mostly identical output, with an occasional run that differs, and it'll differ on exactly the inputs where the decision was close."
2 · Trace the mechanism "Temperature zero removes sampling: the decoder takes the top token. It doesn't make the arithmetic reproducible. My request is batched with other traffic, floating-point addition isn't associative, so the logits can differ in their last bits from run to run."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is: the output changes only when two candidate tokens are nearly tied. Then a last-bit difference flips the top token, and everything generated after it follows the new path."
4 · Variants that flip it "A seed only fixes the sampler, and at temperature zero there's nothing left to sample. What does give bitwise repeatability is a pinned model on my own servers with batch-invariant kernels, and that costs throughput. A silent model update on a hosted API breaks it again."
5 · The production version "So I don't promise identical text. I guarantee structure with a schema, I test fields with tolerance, never whole strings, I cache outputs that were approved, and I log the full request and raw response for audit."
Close "Temperature zero makes decoding greedy. Reproducibility is something I design around it."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.claim: mostly the same, sometimes not
stages.html:
"Same prompt, temperature 0, same seed: usually the same text, with rare divergences."

Guarantee On a hosted API How to get it
Identical text no self-hosted, pinned, batch-invariant
Valid structure yes schema-constrained output
Stable decisions measurably an eval set and a release gate
An audit trail yes log request, versions and raw response

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.claim: greedy decoding over non-reproducible logits
stages.html:
"Two sources of variation; temperature removes only the first."

Request path:promptbatched with other requestskernels sum in an order that depends on the batchlogits differ in the last bitsargmax
(a + b) + c  ≠  a + (b + c)      ← floating-point addition is not associative
Source Removed by temperature 0?
Sampling from the distribution yes
Batch-dependent arithmetic order no
Different hardware or replicas no
A provider-side model or runtime update no

The model-side detail is in temperature-zero-still-varies.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: a near-tie flips one token
stages.html:
"The last bits matter only when the top two tokens are almost equal."

a, b = (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3, 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3)        # same three numbers, two summation orders
print(a, b, a == b)                                # → 0.6000000000000001 0.6 False
for name, approve in (("order A", a), ("order B", b)):
    logits = {"reject": 0.6, "approve": approve}   # a near-tie between two tokens
    print(name, max(logits, key=logits.get))       # → order A approve
                                                   # → order B reject

The tie is constructed to show the mechanism. In real traffic it's rare, load-dependent, and concentrated on marginal inputs, which is why it shows up as a bug report nobody can reproduce.

After the flip:one different tokena different prefixevery later token conditioned on ita visibly different answer

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: what a seed and a pinned stack do
stages.html:
"Each setting fixes one layer."

Variant Effect on reproducibility
Add a seed at temperature 0 none: nothing is sampled
Seed at temperature above 0 fixes the sampler; logits still vary, so "mostly the same"
Pin the model snapshot removes silent model updates
Batch size 1, or batch-invariant kernels (self-hosted) bitwise repeatable, at lower throughput
A different replica or GPU type can differ again

Some hosted APIs return a fingerprint of the backend configuration; when it changes, outputs may change. That's a best-effort signal, not a guarantee, as of 2026.

stages.name: The production version
stages.claim: guarantee structure, test with tolerance
stages.html:
"I move the guarantee from the text to the things the business depends on."

Need Design
The same shape every time schema-constrained output
The same decision eval set; a gate on the flip rate between repeated runs
Tests that don't flake assert on fields, enums and ranges, not on strings
The same answer shown twice store the approved output and serve it; don't regenerate
Audit log prompt version, model version, parameters and the raw response

Temperature 0 is right for extraction and classification. On generative tasks it gives flat text, and it switches off self-consistency.

Fix layer: infra/serving for determinism, application for caching and tests.

followUps.question: "Set temperature 0 and a seed, and the regression test compares strings."
followUps.html:
That test will fail at random.

String comparison Field comparison
Fails on a harmless rewording passes if the decision is the same
Flakes with load stable
Gets disabled within a month stays on as a gate

followUps.question: 🧪 A classifier at temperature 0 gives the same label on 995 of 1,000 repeated runs of one input. Is that a bug?
followUps.html:
No. It's a near-tie input, and the 0.5% is the measurement of it.

flip rate = 5 / 1,000 = 0.5% on this input     ← the top two labels are almost equal
action: treat it as low-confidence, not as an outage

Those inputs are candidates for a clearer rule, an example, or human review.

followUps.question: A regulator asks you to reproduce a decision from six months ago. Can you?
followUps.html:
I can show it, not re-run it.

  • Stored: the rendered prompt, model and prompt versions, parameters and the raw response.
  • Not promised: that a re-run today gives the same text; the model may no longer exist.
  • So: the record is the evidence, and decisions that matter are stored, not regenerated.

followUps.question: Does prompt caching add variation?
followUps.html:
No. It reuses computation for identical input tokens.

Changes the output?
Provider prefix cache no
Your own response cache it removes variation: same request, stored answer

followUps.question: When would you pay for bitwise reproducibility?
followUps.html:
When a test or a contract depends on it, and I run the stack.

Requirements:self-hosted modelpinned weights and runtimebatch-invariant modefixed seedaccept lower throughput

dontSay: "Temperature 0 is deterministic." — it's greedy; the logits can still differ.
"We set a seed, so it's reproducible." — the seed controls a sampler that isn't being used.
"Our tests compare the output to a golden string." — compare fields.
"It's a provider bug." — it's floating point and batching, working as designed.

spine: Where RAG or a tool wins
What I'd pick, and in what order
prompt-engineering-q16.testing: that you diagnose the gap before choosing the lever, and reach for the cheapest one that closes it.
prompt-engineering-q16.trap: "Fine-tune it on our data so it knows our products."
prompt-engineering-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "These four aren't alternatives on one scale. Each fixes a different gap, so I ask first: is the model missing instructions, missing knowledge, missing an ability to act, or missing a consistent behaviour?"
2 · Where prompting wins "If the model can already do the task and just isn't doing it my way, that's a prompt. It's free to iterate and I can ship a change in minutes."
3 · Where RAG or a tool wins "If the gap is knowledge that changes or needs a citation, that's retrieval. If it's something the model shouldn't guess, live data, arithmetic, or a write, that's a tool."
4 · Where fine-tuning wins "Fine-tuning is for behaviour that's stable and high-volume: a strict format, a tone, or getting a small model to do what a large one does with a long prompt."
5 · What I'd pick, and in what order "So the order is prompt first, then retrieval or tools, then a fine-tune only when the eval shows a behaviour gap that prompting can't close. In production it's usually a combination."
Close "The lever follows from the gap, and the eval set tells me which gap I have."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: four levers for four different gaps
stages.html:
"Diagnose the gap first; the lever follows."

The model is missing Lever Changes
Instructions for this request prompt the context, per call
Facts that change or need a source RAG the context, from an index
The ability to look up, compute or act tool what the system can do
A stable behaviour, at volume fine-tune the weights

Why this matters: teams that skip the diagnosis fix a knowledge gap with training, or a behaviour gap with more documents.

stages.name: Where prompting wins
stages.claim: the capability is there, the behaviour isn't
stages.html:
"If a clear instruction and two examples get close, stay with the prompt."

Signal Why a prompt is enough
The model does it right sometimes the ability exists; it needs steering
Requirements still changing a prompt changes in minutes, with no training run
Low or moderate volume prompt tokens are cheaper than a training pipeline

Limit: every call pays for the prompt's tokens, and long prompts drift into contradiction.

stages.name: Where RAG or a tool wins
stages.claim: knowledge and action don't belong in weights
stages.html:
"Anything that changes, needs attribution, or must be exact comes from outside the model."

Need Lever Because
Company documents, policies RAG re-index on change; cite the source
Per-user permissions RAG enforced at retrieval
Live data (stock, order status) tool the model can't know it
Arithmetic, date maths tool exact, not predicted
Writes (refund, email) tool, with approval an action needs a controlled path

stages.name: Where fine-tuning wins
stages.claim: stable behaviour at volume
stages.html:
"Fine-tune behaviour, not knowledge."

Good reason Bad reason
A strict format or tone the prompt can't hold "so it knows our docs"
A small model replacing a large one plus a long prompt facts that change monthly
A narrow task at high volume the prompt hasn't been tried properly

Costs to state: training data, an eval for regressions, and a retrain on every base-model upgrade.

stages.name: What I'd pick, and in what order
stages.claim: cheapest lever first, then combine
stages.html:
"Prompt, then retrieval and tools, then a targeted fine-tune."

Order of moves:prompt + eval setadd RAGadd a toolfine-tune

Prove it — the comparison I'd run, never a guess:

Setup Answer quality Faithfulness Cost per query p95 latency
Prompt only measure measure measure measure
Prompt + RAG measure measure measure measure
+ tool for lookups measure measure measure measure
+ fine-tuned generator measure measure measure measure

Each row is added only if the row above leaves a gap on the golden set.

followUps.question: 🧪 A support bot must quote today's refund policy, check an order's status, and always answer in a three-part format. Which lever for each?
followUps.html:
Three needs, three levers.

Need Lever
Today's refund policy RAG: re-indexed when the policy changes, cited
Order status a read-only tool
Three-part format prompt with a schema; fine-tune only if it still drifts

followUps.question: "Fine-tune it on our documents so it knows them."
followUps.html:
That's a knowledge gap, so it's retrieval.

A fine-tune on documents
Facts learned unreliably
Citations none
When a document changes stale until retrained
Deleting one customer's data not possible without retraining

followUps.question: When does a longer prompt stop being the right answer?
followUps.html:
When it's long because it holds knowledge, or long because it holds patches.

The prompt is long because Move it to
It carries reference material retrieval
It carries dozens of examples retrieved examples, or a fine-tune
It carries a rule per incident a rewrite against an eval set

followUps.question: How do the levers combine in one system?
followUps.html:
Each does its own job.

One request:system prompt (policy and format)retrieved context (knowledge)tool calls (live data, actions)a generator, fine-tuned only if needed

followUps.question: Leadership asks why you aren't training your own model. Answer.
followUps.html:
Because the advantage is in our data and workflow, not in weights.

Investment Return
Eval set on our tasks durable; survives every model change
Retrieval over our content our knowledge, current and permissioned
A targeted fine-tune only where the eval shows it pays
Our own base model high cost, no edge over available models

dontSay: "Fine-tune it so it knows our data." — knowledge belongs in retrieval.
"RAG fixes hallucination." — it supplies evidence; grounding still has to be checked.
"We'll do all four." — say which gap each one closes.
"Prompting is just a stopgap." — it's the first lever and often the last one needed.

spine: Where repair loops earn their place
prompt-engineering-q17.testing: that you separate "parses", "matches the schema" and "is correct", and put a control at each level.
prompt-engineering-q17.trap: "We use structured outputs, so the data is correct."
prompt-engineering-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "There are three different guarantees: the output parses, the output has my shape, and the values are right. Each technique gives a different one."
2 · Where JSON mode is enough "JSON mode only guarantees parseable JSON. That's fine for loose, exploratory output, or where my own code tolerates missing keys."
3 · Where schema-constrained wins "Schema-constrained decoding compiles my schema into a grammar and masks illegal tokens, so the shape is right by construction. That's my default for anything code consumes."
4 · Where repair loops earn their place "Neither of those checks meaning. So I validate the values, and when validation fails I feed the specific error back once or twice. That works because the model gets new information; it's not a blind retry."
5 · What I'd ship "So I ship all three layers: constrain the shape, validate the meaning, repair within a budget, and return a typed failure when the budget runs out. And I count repairs as a metric."
Close "Shape is the provider's job; correctness stays mine."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: parses, has the shape, is correct
stages.html:
"Three guarantees, and no single technique gives all three."

Technique Parses Your keys, types, enums Values are right
Prompt: "reply in JSON" usually no no
JSON mode no no
Schema-constrained decoding no
+ validation and repair the rules you encoded

stages.name: Where JSON mode is enough
stages.claim: loose output, tolerant consumer
stages.html:
"JSON mode is fine when nothing downstream depends on exact fields."

Fits Doesn't fit
Exploration, prototypes anything written to a database
A consumer that handles missing keys tool arguments
Providers or models without schema support enums the business depends on

stages.name: Where schema-constrained wins
stages.claim: shape by construction
stages.html:
"The grammar makes an illegal token unreachable, not just unlikely."

Per token:schema compiled to a grammarcurrent statemask tokens that can't continue itsample from what's left
The guarantee is void when What you get
The model refuses a refusal, not your object
max_tokens is hit mid-object a truncated object
The schema uses unsupported features an error, or a silent fallback

Also: forcing the answer field first removes the model's room to reason. Put a reasoning field before it.

stages.name: Where repair loops earn their place
stages.claim: meaning, with a budget
stages.html:
"A repair is a re-ask with the validation error, which is new information."

import json
REPLIES = ['{"status": "Closed", "priority": 2}', '{"status": "closed", "priority": 2}']   # scripted model
def validate(obj):
    if obj.get("status") not in ("open", "closed"): return "status must be 'open' or 'closed'"
    if not isinstance(obj.get("priority"), int): return "priority must be an integer"
def call(max_repairs=1):
    error = None
    for attempt in range(max_repairs + 1):
        obj = json.loads(REPLIES[attempt])                    # parses both times: JSON mode is satisfied
        error = validate(obj)
        if error is None: return f"ok after {attempt} repair(s): {obj}"
        print(f"attempt {attempt}: parsed, but invalid -> re-ask with: {error}")
    return f"typed failure: {error}"
print(call())
# → attempt 0: parsed, but invalid -> re-ask with: status must be 'open' or 'closed'
# → ok after 1 repair(s): {'status': 'closed', 'priority': 2}

The first reply is valid JSON and still wrong. With an enum in a constrained schema, that first failure can't happen; the loop then only handles rules a schema can't express.

stages.name: What I'd ship
stages.claim: constrain, validate, repair once, fail typed
stages.html:
"Layers, each with a metric."

Path:schema-constrained callcheck finish reasonvalidate valuesone repair with the errortyped failure or fallback model
Metric Why
Schema-failure rate should be near zero with constraints
Repair rate, per prompt version a rising rate is quality drift you'd otherwise never see
Truncation rate points at max_tokens or verbose fields

Fix layer: shape in infra/serving, meaning in application validation, the rest in the prompt.

followUps.question: 🧪 In the snippet, what happens with ?
followUps.html:
One attempt, then a typed failure.

attempt 0: parsed, but invalid -> re-ask with: status must be 'open' or 'closed'
typed failure: status must be 'open' or 'closed'

The caller gets an error it can handle, not a wrong object that looks fine.

followUps.question: "A tolerant parser that fixes small mistakes is the pragmatic choice."
followUps.html:
Silent repair hides the metric you most need.

Tolerant parser Counted repair
Failures disappear failures are a number
Quality drifts unseen drift shows per prompt and model version
A model upgrade looks fine a model upgrade shows its regressions

followUps.question: Does constraining the output cost quality?
followUps.html:
It can, when the format leaves no room to reason.

Fix How
Field order a free-text reasoning field before the answer
Two calls reason freely, then format
Simpler schema fewer nested and optional parts

followUps.question: What does a schema not express?
followUps.html:
Anything that depends on other data.

Schema can say Schema can't say
status is one of two values the status matches the ticket
amount is a number the amount appears in the source document
date is a string in a format the date is in the future

followUps.question: Structured output fails 2% of the time at a million calls a day. What do you do?
followUps.html:
Find the dominant cause before adding retries: 2% is twenty thousand failures a day.

Cause Fix
Truncation raise max_tokens, shorten fields
Unsupported schema features simplify the schema
Semantic validation better instructions or examples
Then:one repairfallback modeltyped failure, with the rate tracked per prompt version.

dontSay: "Structured outputs guarantee correct data." — shape only.
"I regex the JSON out of the reply." — constrain at decode time.
"Retry until it parses." — unbounded, and it never checks meaning.
"Our parser is forgiving." — that's silent repair.

links.label: Why structured output is a systems problem
links.target: 08-Prompt-engineering/04-Structured Output & Control/35-Why structured output is a systems problem

prompt-engineering-q18.testing: that you split for testability, know the latency and compounding-error bill, and don't call a fixed chain an agent.
prompt-engineering-q18.trap: chaining by default, or describing a chain you designed as "an agent".
prompt-engineering-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The question is how many jobs one call is doing. A chain splits one prompt into staged calls where each output feeds the next. It trades latency and moving parts for control and testability."
2 · Where one prompt wins "One prompt wins when the task is one job, or the latency budget is tight. It's one call, one cache prefix, and nothing to orchestrate."
3 · Where a chain wins "A chain wins when a single prompt is holding several jobs, like extract, then judge, then draft. Each stage gets a focused context, its own eval, its own retry policy, and often a cheaper model."
4 · The deciding question "My test for where to cut is: can I write a test for the intermediate output? If I can check the extraction on its own, that's a good boundary. If I can't say what a correct intermediate result is, the split is arbitrary."
5 · What I'd pick "I start with one prompt and an eval. I split only where the eval shows a stage failing, I run independent stages in parallel, and I validate between stages, because errors compound: three stages at ninety-five percent each is about eighty-six percent end to end."
Close "One job per call, a test per stage, and a budget for the latency I've added."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: jobs per call
stages.html:
"Four shapes, ordered by how much the path is fixed in advance."

Approach Who decides the next step Latency Debugging
Single prompt nobody: one step lowest one output, one blob of failure
Fixed chain I did, at design time adds per stage per-stage evals and retries
Conditional chain my code, by a branch varies by path per-branch evals
Agent loop the model, at run time unbounded hardest: the path varies per run

A chain is a fixed graph I designed. An agent chooses its own next step. Calling the first one the second sets the wrong expectations for testing and cost.

stages.name: Where one prompt wins
stages.claim: one job, tight latency
stages.html:
"If it's one job, splitting only adds latency and failure points."

Fits Because
A single transformation (classify, extract, rewrite) nothing intermediate to test
A sub-second budget every stage adds a full round trip
A reasoning model on a multi-step problem it plans internally; my scaffold can get in its way
Steps that need each other's full context a hand-off would lose information

stages.name: Where a chain wins
stages.claim: focused context and a test per stage
stages.html:
"Splitting pays when the jobs have different inputs, different failure modes or different difficulty."

Chain:ticketextract fields (small model, schema)validatejudge policy (strong model)draft reply (mid model)
What a stage gets Why it matters
Its own context the drafter doesn't read the raw 20-page thread
Its own eval "extraction is 98%, policy is 85%" tells me where to work
Its own retry and fallback a failed extraction retries without redoing the draft
Its own model easy stages run on a cheaper model

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: can I test the intermediate output
stages.html:
"A good boundary is one where the hand-off has a schema and a definition of correct."

Candidate cut Testable hand-off? Verdict
Extract → decide yes: fields against labels split
Retrieve → answer yes: retrieved set against relevant set split
"Think" → "answer" no clear definition of a correct thought keep together, or use a reasoning field
Draft → polish only by judgement split only if the eval shows a gain

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: split on evidence, validate between stages
stages.html:
"The bill for a chain is computable, so I compute it."

end-to-end success = product of the stage success rates     (illustrative rates)
3 stages × 0.95  → 0.95³ = 0.857     ← 86%, not 95%
4 stages × 0.90  → 0.90⁴ = 0.656
latency          = sum of the serial stages; parallel stages cost the slowest one
Rule Why
Validate each hand-off (schema + checks) a caught error can be retried; an uncaught one compounds
Run independent stages in parallel latency of the slowest, not the sum
Trace by request id across stages with prompt and model version per stage
One eval per stage, plus end to end each stage's prompt is tuned to its own model

Fix layer: orchestration for the chain, prompt/context per stage.

followUps.question: "We built an agent: it extracts, then classifies, then drafts."
followUps.html:
That's a chain, and that's the better news.

Chain Agent
Steps fixed by you chosen by the model
Cost per request bounded variable
Testing per stage per trajectory

Use an agent only when the steps can't be known in advance.

followUps.question: 🧪 Five stages at 95% each. What's the end-to-end rate, and what improves it most?
followUps.html:
About 77%, and validation between stages improves it more than a better prompt in one stage.

0.95⁵ = 0.774                       ← with no checks between stages
with a check + one retry per stage: a stage fails only if both tries fail
0.05² = 0.0025 per stage → (1 − 0.0025)⁵ ≈ 0.988    ← if the check catches every error

Real checks miss some errors, so the true figure sits between the two.

followUps.question: Doesn't a chain multiply cost?
followUps.html:
Not necessarily: more calls, but smaller contexts and cheaper models.

  • Up: per-call overhead, repeated instructions, more output tokens in total.
  • Down: each stage reads only what it needs; easy stages use a small model.
  • So: measure tokens per stage; don't assume either way.

followUps.question: How do you debug a chain?
followUps.html:
From the first stage whose output fails its own check.

Path:failing requesttrace by idfirst invalid hand-offrendered prompt of that stageadd the case to that stage's eval

followUps.question: When would you collapse a chain back into one prompt?
followUps.html:
When a newer model does the whole job as well in one call.

Signal Action
After an upgrade, the single-prompt eval matches the chain collapse; drop the latency and the orchestration
A stage's eval is at ceiling on a small model keep it; it's cheap

Scaffolding built for a weaker model is the first thing to re-test on an upgrade.

dontSay: "We chain everything for quality." — say which stage failed in one prompt.
"It's an agent." — if you wrote the steps, it's a chain.
"Each step is 95% accurate, so the system is." — the rates multiply.
"Chaining is slower, so we avoid it." — independent stages run in parallel.

prompt-engineering-q19.testing: that you know the prompting style reverses between the two, and that reasoning is a budget you route, not a default.
prompt-engineering-q19.trap: porting a "think step by step" prompt unchanged to a reasoning model.
prompt-engineering-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both options spend extra tokens before the answer. The difference is who manages the reasoning: my prompt, or the model's own thinking phase. That changes how I write the prompt and what I pay."
2 · Where the reasoning model wins "A reasoning model wins on hard, multi-step problems where a wrong answer is expensive: planning, tricky analysis, code with interacting constraints. I give it the goal, the constraints and what a good answer looks like, and I don't prescribe steps."
3 · Where the standard model wins "A standard model with a prompted scaffold still wins on cheap, well-understood tasks at volume, and on anything latency-sensitive. Most classification and extraction needs no reasoning at all."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask two things: does reasoning change the answer on this slice, according to the eval? And can the user wait for it? Thinking tokens are output tokens, generated one after another."
5 · What I'd pick "I route by difficulty. Easy requests take the standard model with a direct prompt; hard ones take the reasoning model with a short prompt and a thinking budget. And I keep two prompts, because one prompt doesn't suit both."
Close "Reasoning is a dial with a bill, so I turn it only where the eval says it pays."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: who manages the reasoning
stages.html:
"Prompted chain-of-thought and a reasoning model buy the same thing, compute before the answer, from different places."

Standard model + prompted CoT Reasoning model
Who plans the steps my prompt the model's thinking phase
The dial how much scaffold I write a thinking budget or effort setting
The prompt steps, examples, format goal, constraints, success criteria
The bill visible output tokens thinking tokens and latency
Pick when cheap, well-understood, high volume hard, and errors are costly

Why extra tokens help at all is in why-cot-works.

stages.name: Where the reasoning model wins
stages.claim: hard problems, goal-only prompts
stages.html:
"On a reasoning model the prompting change is subtractive."

Prompt element Standard model Reasoning model
"Think step by step" can help on multi-step tasks redundant or harmful
A prescribed decomposition often needed narrows how it reasons; remove it
Goal and success criteria useful the main content of the prompt
Constraints and output contract needed still needed

Vendor guidance as of 2026 says the same: state what you want and how it'll be judged, and let the model allocate its own reasoning.

stages.name: Where the standard model wins
stages.claim: cheap tasks and tight latency
stages.html:
"The latency of reasoning is simple arithmetic."

assume 50 output tokens per second (illustrative)
direct answer on a standard model:     5 tokens             →  0.1 s
prompted chain-of-thought:           200 + 5 tokens         →  4.1 s
reasoning model:                   2,000 thinking + 5       → 40 s      ← if it uses that much
Fits the standard model Because
Classification, extraction, lookup reasoning adds cost, little accuracy
Interactive paths the user waits for every thinking token
A task whose steps I know a short scaffold is predictable and cheap

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does reasoning change the answer here
stages.html:
"I measure it per slice; I don't decide by the task's reputation."

Slice of the eval Standard, direct Standard + CoT Reasoning model
Easy (accuracy · latency · cost) measure measure measure
Multi-step measure measure measure
Hard, high-stakes measure measure measure

A thinking budget is a target, not a cap: usage varies widely by input, and max_tokens is the real ceiling, shared with the answer. So I plan capacity on the distribution of thinking tokens, not on the mean.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: route by difficulty, two prompts
stages.html:
"A router keeps the reasoning bill on the requests that need it."

Routing:requestdifficulty estimatestandard model, direct promptreasoning model, goal-only prompt + budget
10% hard at 40 s, 90% easy at 0.1 s (illustrative)
mean wait = 0.1 × 40 + 0.9 × 0.1 = 4.09 s     ← against 40 s if everything took the reasoning path
Rule Why
Two prompts, one per model a prompt is tuned to one model
Watch under-routing a hard request on the cheap path gives a confident wrong answer
Re-check on every model generation budget parameters and thinking behaviour change

Fix layer: model choice and orchestration for the router; prompt/context for the two prompts.

followUps.question: "Add 'think step by step' to the reasoning model too. More thinking can't hurt."
followUps.html:
It can: it constrains reasoning the model already does, and adds visible output.

On a reasoning model Effect
Prescribed steps the model follows my plan, not a better one
"Show your reasoning" extra output tokens on top of thinking tokens
A removed scaffold often equal or better; measure it

followUps.question: 🧪 Thinking budget 8,000,  8,500, and the answer needs 1,200 tokens. What can go wrong?
followUps.html:
The answer can be cut off.

8,500 total − up to 8,000 thinking = as little as 500 left for the answer
needed: 1,200                          ← truncated on inputs that think long
fix: max_tokens ≥ budget + the longest answer, and check the finish reason

followUps.question: Can you show the model's thinking to users as the explanation?
followUps.html:
No. It isn't a faithful record of how the answer was produced.

  • Show: sources and checkable facts.
  • Log: inputs, outputs and versions for audit.

followUps.question: How does the router estimate difficulty?
followUps.html:
Start with rules, and move up only when they plateau.

Router Added latency
Static rules (endpoint, customer tier) none
Request features (length, entity count) negligible
A small classifier one small call
Cascade: try cheap, escalate on a failed check an extra call only on escalation

followUps.question: How do you budget for a reasoning model at scale?
followUps.html:
On the tail of the thinking-token distribution, per route.

  • Capacity and cost: p95 of thinking tokens, not the mean.
  • Latency: a time-out with a fallback to the standard path.
  • A signal: requests that hit the budget ceiling are candidates for a higher band.

dontSay: "We use the reasoning model for everything, to be safe." — most traffic pays and doesn't gain.
"Same prompt, just a different model name." — the prompting style reverses.
"The budget caps the cost." — it's a target; max_tokens is the cap.
"Reasoning models are always more accurate." — on easy tasks the difference is in the bill.

prompt-engineering-q20.testing: that you see an optimisation run as an inference workload with a bounded, decaying benefit, and that the eval harness comes first either way.
prompt-engineering-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both are searches over prompt text. One is a person reading outputs; the other is a program scoring candidates against a metric. So the real question is whether I have a metric worth searching against, and whether the prompt lives long enough to repay the search."
2 · Where hand-tuning wins "Hand-tuning wins early, when the task is still changing, when traffic is low, and when the failures are structural. A missing tool or bad retrieval isn't something a search over wording can fix."
3 · Where auto-optimisation wins "Auto-optimisation wins on stable, high-traffic prompts, and most of all on multi-step pipelines, where instructions and examples multiply across steps and no person can sweep the combinations."
4 · The deciding question "I ask three things. Is there a metric I trust? Is the prompt stable for months? And is the traffic high enough that a few points matter? A run can be tens of thousands of model calls, and the gain fades when the model changes."
5 · What I'd pick "So the order is: build the eval, hand-tune to a sensible baseline, then optimise only the stable, high-volume prompts, with a held-out set. After a model upgrade I recompile."
Close "The eval set and the metric are the assets I keep; the optimised prompt is disposable."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: two searches over the same space
stages.html:
"Hand-tuning fails in three specific ways, and each has a mechanical answer."

Hand-tuning breaks on Why What an optimiser does
A combinatorial space instructions × examples × steps is a product samples it with a search
Noise read as signal twenty outputs, eyeballed scores every candidate on a fixed set
Regressions on old cases each edit is untested and non-local re-scores the full set every time
One person's intuitions the reasons live in someone's head the artefact is data + metric + a compile step 
3 steps, each with 5 candidate instructions × 4 example sets = 20 options per step
combinations = 20 × 20 × 20 = 8,000        ← nobody sweeps that by hand

stages.name: Where hand-tuning wins
stages.claim: early, low-traffic, structural
stages.html:
"A person is the right optimiser when the problem isn't wording."

Situation Why hand-tune
No metric yet there's nothing to optimise against
The task changes weekly every change invalidates a run
Low traffic the run costs more than the gain is worth
Structural failures search can't invent a missing tool or fix retrieval
A model upgrade is close optimise after it, not before

Reading failures by hand is also how I learn what the metric should be.

stages.name: Where auto-optimisation wins
stages.claim: stable, high-volume, multi-step
stages.html:
"Compute is cheaper than attention when the target holds still."

Run:trainset + metricgenerate candidatesscore each on the trainsetkeep the bestcheck on a held-out set
Fits Because
High traffic, stable task a few points compound over volume
A multi-step pipeline hand-tuning is weakest exactly there
Frequent model changes with a fixed task recompiling beats re-tuning by hand

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: is the search worth its bill
stages.html:
"I price the run before I start it."

calls = candidates × trials × trainset size × calls per example      (illustrative)
      = 30 trials × 200 examples × 2 steps = 12,000 model calls per run
benefit: a few metric points, on one model, until the model or the task changes
Question If no
Do I trust the metric? fix the metric; an optimiser will game a bad one
Stable for months? hand-tune
Enough traffic for the points to matter? hand-tune
Is the failure about wording? do failure analysis first

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: harness, baseline, then optimise selectively
stages.html:
"The same three steps in the same order, whatever the tool."

Order:build the evalhand-tune a baselineoptimise stable high-volume promptsgate on held-outrecompile on model change
Variant Held-out metric Tokens per call
Hand-tuned baseline measure measure
Optimised measure measure

The optimised prompt is versioned, traced and reviewed like any other. Its extra examples change the token count and the cached prefix, so cost is part of the comparison.

Fix layer: prompt/context, produced by tooling; the gate is eval.

followUps.question: "Let's run the optimiser first and build evals later."
followUps.html:
There's nothing for it to optimise.

Wrong order:optimiserno metricoptimises a proxyconfident, wrong prompt
Right order:metric validated against peoplebaselineoptimiserheld-out check

followUps.question: 🧪 The optimiser gains 4 points on 100 training examples. Do you ship?
followUps.html:
Not on that evidence.

SE at p ≈ 0.8, n = 100: √(0.8 × 0.2 / 100) = 0.04      ← ±8 points at 95%
a 4-point gain, on the set it was tuned on              ← inside the noise, and optimistic

I'd look at a held-out set, larger and paired.

followUps.question: What does an optimiser not fix?
followUps.html:
Anything outside the prompt text.

  • Missing knowledge: needs retrieval.
  • Missing capability or tool: needs a model or a tool.
  • A wrong metric: it'll optimise it faithfully.

followUps.question: How does the result survive a model upgrade?
followUps.html:
It doesn't; the inputs to the run do.

Survives Doesn't
Trainset, held-out set, metric the optimised instructions and examples
The compile script the gain measured on the old model

followUps.question: How do you justify the engineering time to build the harness?
followUps.html:
It pays without any optimiser: it's the release gate and the upgrade test.

Use of the harness Value
CI for every prompt change regressions caught before users
Model-upgrade comparison a migration measured in days
Optimisation, if ever a search target that already exists

dontSay: "The optimiser found a better prompt." — better on what, held out, by how much against noise?
"We tune by reading outputs." — fine for learning; not evidence of a gain.
"Optimise everything." — low-traffic and changing prompts never repay the run.
"The compiled prompt is our asset." — the data and the metric are.

prompt-engineering-q21.testing: that you know placement only matters at length, and can resolve the tension between attention (instruction last) and caching (stable text first).
prompt-engineering-q21.trap: burying the question above twenty thousand tokens of documents.
prompt-engineering-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "In a short prompt placement is noise. In a long one it matters, because the model uses the start and the end of its context more reliably than the middle."
2 · Where the top wins "The top is right for stable framing: role, constraints, the output contract. It's the same on every call, so it's also what the cache needs first."
3 · Where the bottom wins "The bottom is right for the specific question and the task instruction. They're read last, right before generation, and they change per request anyway."
4 · The deciding question "So I split the instruction by stability. Is this sentence the same on every request? Then it goes on top. Is it about this request? Then it goes after the documents."
5 · What I'd pick "My layout is policy on top, documents in the middle, question at the bottom, and I repeat the one constraint I can't afford to lose at both ends. Then I check it on the eval with long inputs."
Close "Stable policy first, the question last, and the critical rule twice."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: it only matters at length
stages.html:
"The effect grows with the distance an instruction has to survive."

At a few hundred tokens nothing is far from anything, and position tests as noise.

stages.name: Where the top wins
stages.claim: stable framing, cached
stages.html:
"What's identical on every call goes first."

Content Why the top
Tool definitions large, stable, first in the cache hierarchy
Role, constraints, output contract framing, not the per-request ask
Fixed examples cached with the prefix

A prefix cache matches from the first token, so stable text on top is also a cost decision.

stages.name: Where the bottom wins
stages.claim: the ask, next to generation
stages.html:
"What the model reads last shapes the first tokens it writes."

Layout:tools + system policy<documents> … </documents>the question + the task instructiongeneration
Content Why the bottom
The user's question adjacent to generation; volatile anyway
"Quote the supporting passage first" it shapes the opening tokens
A per-request format ask not lost above the documents

Documents-before-query is also the long-context guidance vendors publish, as of 2026.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: is this sentence stable or per-request
stages.html:
"The two forces pull one instruction in different directions, so I split it."

Force Wants So
Attention at length the instruction last per-request ask goes at the bottom
Prefix caching stable text first policy goes on top
Both a critical rule that mustn't be lost state it at both ends

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: policy on top, question last, sandwich the critical rule
stages.html:
"Then I let the eval confirm it on long inputs."

Layout Accuracy on long-input cases Cache-read share
Everything on top, documents last measure measure
Policy on top, question at the bottom measure measure
Same, critical rule repeated at the end measure measure

The repeat costs a few tokens per call. The best layout is tuned to one model, so the comparison runs again on an upgrade. Longer-term, the better fix is less context: retrieve less and rank better, covered in MCP-CONTEXT-ENGINEERING.

Fix layer: prompt/context.

followUps.question: "The model has a million-token window, so position doesn't matter."
followUps.html:
A window is how much fits, not how evenly it's used.

Claim Reality
It fits, so it's read equally use still varies with position and length
More context is safer more distractors for the same question

followUps.question: 🧪 The system prompt holds the policy and today's question. What's wrong?
followUps.html:
Both problems at once.

question in the system prompt  → the prefix changes on every call   ← cache miss
question above the documents   → furthest from generation           ← weakest position
fix: policy stays on top; the question moves below the documents

followUps.question: Where do the retrieved documents go, and in what order?
followUps.html:
After the policy, before the question, with the strongest ones at the edges.

  • Order: best-ranked chunks first and last, weaker ones in the middle.
  • Fewer: five good chunks beat twenty mixed ones.

followUps.question: Does repeating an instruction ever hurt?
followUps.html:
Only when the two copies drift apart.

Safe Risky
One critical rule, same wording, both ends the whole policy pasted twice
Rendered from one template variable two hand-edited copies

followUps.question: In a multi-turn chat, where does the standing instruction go?
followUps.html:
In the system prompt, with the objective re-pinned as the history grows.

Long session:system policy (cached)summarised middlelast turnspinned objectivecurrent turn

The system text ends up far from generation by turn thirty, so the current objective is restated near the end.

dontSay: "Always put instructions first." — at length, the ask belongs last.
"Always put instructions last." — stable policy on top is what the cache needs.
"Position doesn't matter with modern models." — it matters less, and still measurably at length.
"We put everything in twice." — only the rule you can't lose, from one source.
